summary: The note examines how interruptions to electricity, water, and internet service expose vulnerabilities in healthcare facilities, drawing on incidents from 2023 and 2024. It describes the resulting responses: stronger backup systems, staff drills, policy proposals, new technology, mutual aid, and climate adaptation. It concludes that continuous adaptation and training are essential for resilient healthcare.
one_line: Overview of how utility and internet outages in 2023-2024 affected healthcare facilities and the preparedness, policy, and technology responses that followed.
key_facts: On September 16, 2023, St. Martha's Hospital in downtown experienced a power outage lasting six hours; emergency generators kicked in but revealed capacity gaps for prolonged outages.
Dr. Rebecca Smith, attending physician at St. Martha's, said the outage strained ventilators and some surgeries had to be postponed.
On November 5, 2023, a regional hospital lost internet connectivity due to a cyber-attack, leaving doctors unable to access patient records or digital imaging.
Julia Hernandez, an IT specialist, said the hospital is working on enhancing offline capabilities and backup systems after the cyber-attack.
In December 2023, an unprecedented ice storm knocked out power and water services in several northeastern healthcare facilities, prompting a review of emergency protocols and resource management.
Hospitals like St. Martha's are investing in more robust backup systems, conducting regular stress tests, and exploring mobile and pop-up clinics that operate independent of the main grid.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) recommends comprehensive contingency plans, including sufficiently maintained emergency power supplies.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) collaborates with healthcare providers on drills, simulated service interruptions, and improved communication channels.
Dr. James O'Connor, an emergency room director, said his teams now hold quarterly drills simulating various outage scenarios.

After a week-long power disruption in July 2024 affecting multiple Midwest hospitals, lawmakers led by Senator Elizabeth Warren proposed legislation to increase funding for healthcare resilience projects.
Technologies cited for mitigating outages include smart grids, distributed energy systems, AI-driven predictive maintenance, and renewable energy integration, per engineer Daniel Franklin.

In August 2024, a water main break jeopardized sanitation at Riverside Clinic, and neighboring facilities provided sterile equipment and accepted patient transfers, highlighting the need for mutual aid agreements.
Climate change is making extreme weather more frequent and severe; incorporating green infrastructure can reduce the burden on utility services during such episodes.
